passage:
Coach's note, Cooking Club. Written by Siddharth.
This week some boys teased Amandeep (11) for joining cooking club, saying it was for girls. He didn't get angry; he said, "Everyone eats, so everyone can cook." When we made rotis, he asked the girls at his table before taking their rolling pin, and when one said, "Wait, I'm using it," he waited. Later, when a boy grabbed a girl's plait as a joke, Amandeep said, "She doesn't like that. Stop." The boy stopped.
Next: I will ask Amandeep to help me plan next week's pairs, mixing boys and girls.

qa.q: What did Amandeep say when boys teased him about cooking?
qa.a: He said, "Everyone eats, so everyone can cook."

qa.q: What does Amandeep waiting for the rolling pin suggest about him?
qa.a: It suggests he respects others' boundaries and doesn't just take what he wants.

qa.q: How does Siddharth plan to build on Amandeep's example?
qa.a: Siddharth plans to ask Amandeep to help plan mixed pairs of boys and girls.

qa.q: How might the girl whose plait was grabbed feel when Amandeep speaks up?
qa.a: She would likely feel relieved and respected that someone stood up for her.

grounding: A coach's note shows a boy practising courtesy and boundaries without stereotyped roles.

passage:
Saturday night
Today in football practice Elizabeth scored twice against our side. Last month I would've said "girls can't kick" like the other boys do. Honestly she's the best on the field. 👏 I told her "nice goal" and she looked surprised, like she expected me to be rude. That made me feel bad about before.
After practice, two boys pulled her cap off and threw it around. She said "give it back" and they laughed. I caught it and gave it to her. I didn't make a big speech. I just thought, she said stop, so stop.
— Kashish

qa.q: How many goals did Elizabeth score today?
qa.a: She scored twice against Kashish's side.

qa.q: Why did Kashish feel bad when Elizabeth looked surprised?
qa.a: He realised she expected him to be rude because of how he and the other boys had acted before.

qa.q: What could Kashish try next time boys mock Elizabeth?
qa.a: He could tell them calmly to stop and, if it keeps happening, tell the coach.

qa.q: How might Elizabeth see Kashish after he returns her cap?
qa.a: She may start to trust him and see him as someone who respects her.

grounding: A diary shows a boy admiring a girl's skill, dropping stereotypes and respecting her boundaries.

passage: In the small-town school yard, Shalini and Arohi turned the headmaster's old cycle upside down to fix its chain. A group of boys gathered. "Girls fixing cycles? Ha!" said one. Arohi ignored him, pushed the chain back onto the gear and spun the pedal. It clicked into place. The boys went quiet. The next day, one of them came over, holding his own bike. "My chain keeps falling off. Can you show me?" Shalini handed him the spanner. "Hold it like this." He listened carefully and thanked them both.

qa.q: Whose old cycle did the girls fix?
qa.a: They fixed the headmaster's old cycle.

qa.q: What does the boy asking for help the next day suggest about his view?
qa.a: It suggests he now admires the girls' skill and has dropped the idea that girls can't fix cycles.

qa.q: What helped change the boys' minds?
qa.a: The girls calmly showed their skill instead of arguing, then taught the boy respectfully.

qa.q: How might Arohi feel when the boys go quiet?
qa.a: She may feel quietly proud that their work spoke for itself.

grounding: It shows respectful interaction across genders, moving beyond stereotyped roles and mockery.

passage: It was woodwork class in a school outside Gothenburg, and the room smelled of pine shavings. Hana, eleven, was sawing a board for her birdhouse. Two boys at the next bench snickered. 'Careful, she'll cut her nails.' Anders, who shared her bench, didn't laugh. He had been about to grab her saw to help, then stopped. 'Want me to hold the board steady, or are you fine?' Hana blew hair out of her eyes. 'Fine. But you can pass the sandpaper.' He passed it. When the boys snickered again, Anders said, 'Her cut is straighter than yours, Olle.' Olle looked at his wobbly board and went quiet. Hana smiled at the sawdust.

qa.q: What was Hana making in woodwork class?
qa.a: She was sawing a board for her birdhouse.

qa.q: How do you think Anders felt when he stopped before grabbing Hana's saw?
qa.a: He seemed hesitant, realising she might not want help and that taking over could look like he thought she couldn't do it.

qa.q: What did Anders do that showed respect?
qa.a: He asked before helping, accepted her 'fine', and calmly answered the teasing with a fact instead of mockery.

qa.q: How might Hana have felt if Anders had laughed along with the boys?
qa.a: She would likely have felt more alone and embarrassed, and less willing to use the tools in front of them.

grounding: Shows courtesy and respect for boundaries between classmates of different genders, without stereotyped roles.

passage: The Saturday embroidery club at the community centre had eleven girls and, from this week, one boy. Anirban, twelve, sat at the end of the long table with a hoop and red thread. Two girls whispered and giggled. 'Did he come for the biscuits?' Dolma, who was helping Mrs Bose hand out needles, heard. She sat down beside him. 'Your chain stitch is neater than mine. Show me?' He showed her, ears pink. Later he reached for her scissors, then stopped. 'Can I borrow these?' 'Sure.' When the giggling started again, Dolma said, 'He's here to stitch, same as us.' The whisperers went back to their flowers.

qa.q: How many girls were in the embroidery club?
qa.a: There were eleven girls.

qa.q: What do Anirban's pink ears suggest he was feeling?
qa.a: He was probably embarrassed by the giggling but also pleased that Dolma asked him to show his stitch.

qa.q: What did Dolma do that a helper could copy?
qa.a: She sat with the new member, praised his real skill, and calmly said he belonged there instead of mocking back.

qa.q: How might the two whispering girls see Anirban after Dolma spoke?
qa.a: They might start seeing him as just another club member rather than someone to laugh at.

grounding: Shows respectful interaction across genders without mockery, including asking before borrowing.

passage:
I'm Disha, in Class 6 with Thomas. I've noticed he's different from some boys in our class.
When he joined the dance group, Varun called him “Thomasina.” Thomas just said, “I like dancing. You like cricket. Both are fine,” and kept practising.
When Gauri from our group was playing football and a boy said girls should go and skip, Thomas passed her the ball.
And when he needed my ruler, he asked first. He didn't just grab it, like others do.
I don't know what goes on in his head. But I trust him more than most.

qa.q: What did Varun call Thomas?
qa.a: He called him “Thomasina.”

qa.q: How did Thomas seem to feel about the teasing?
qa.a: He seemed calm and confident, not hurt enough to stop dancing.

qa.q: What could other boys learn from Thomas?
qa.a: That anyone can dance or play football, and that asking before taking shows respect.

qa.q: How does Disha see Thomas?
qa.a: Disha trusts and admires him more than most classmates.

grounding: A classmate observes an eleven-year-old boy showing courtesy and rejecting gender stereotypes.

passage:
Monday: In the school ground, Harish said, “Girls can't play kabaddi. It's rough.” Uma, ten, felt her face go hot. Gurleen pulled her arm. “Leave it.”
But Uma stepped forward. “We can. Can we try one game?”
Wednesday: The PE teacher set up a mixed game with clear rules: no pushing on the face, stop when someone says stop. Uma raided twice and got Harish out once. Harish laughed. “Okay, okay.”
Next Monday: Harish came up to Uma. “Can you show me that side step?”
Uma grinned. “Only if you show me your ankle hold.”

qa.q: What did Harish say about girls and kabaddi?
qa.a: He said girls can't play kabaddi because it's rough.

qa.q: How did Uma feel when Harish said girls can't play?
qa.a: She felt angry and embarrassed, her face going hot.

qa.q: What helped the boys and girls play respectfully together?
qa.a: A mixed game with clear rules and boundaries, such as stopping when someone says stop.

qa.q: How does Harish's view of Uma change?
qa.a: He moves from doubting girls to respecting Uma's skill and asking her to teach him.

grounding: Over a week a ten-year-old girl challenges a stereotype and builds respectful play with boys.

passage:
Nirmala, you asked if boys teased me when I was your age. Let your Simran Dadi tell you.
When I was twelve, in Jalandhar, a boy named Balwinder used to pull my plait every day in class and laugh. Everyone thought it was funny. I didn't.
One day I turned round and said, “Stop. I don't like it.” He looked shocked. Then he said sorry, and never did it again.
We became good friends, and years later he told me he had never thought about how it felt.
What I learnt, beti: you can say no, clearly and kindly, and a good person listens. Your Dadu listened too.

qa.q: What did Balwinder do every day?
qa.a: He pulled her plait every day in class and laughed.

qa.q: How did young Simran feel about Balwinder pulling her plait?
qa.a: She felt annoyed and upset, not finding it funny.

qa.q: What was the turning point in the story, and why did it work?
qa.a: Simran clearly said “Stop. I don't like it,” which made Balwinder think and respect her boundary.

qa.q: How might Balwinder have felt when Simran told him to stop?
qa.a: He was shocked and then sorry, realising for the first time how it felt for her.

grounding: A grandmother tells how she set a boundary with a boy who teased her, and he respected it.

passage:
The cricket match on the colony ground was cut short by rain, and only one end of the pitch was dry. Parul said, "Let Ritu bowl the last over."
"Girls can't bowl properly," muttered Advait, the captain.
Ritu didn't argue. She took the wet ball, dried it on her shirt, and ran in.
The first ball skidded past Advait's bat.
He stared. Then he said, "Okay, that was good."
"Just say 'nice ball'," said Parul. "Not 'for a girl'."
Advait nodded. "Nice ball, Ritu."
Ritu smiled and bowled the next one.

qa.q: What did Ritu dry the wet ball on?
qa.a: Her shirt.

qa.q: What might Advait have been feeling when he stared?
qa.a: Advait was surprised and a bit embarrassed that his remark was wrong.

qa.q: What did Parul suggest, and why does it matter?
qa.a: She told Advait to just say "nice ball" without "for a girl", which treats Ritu with the same respect as any bowler.

qa.q: How might Ritu feel when Advait finally says "Nice ball, Ritu"?
qa.a: Ritu probably feels respected and proud 🏏 that her skill was recognised without mockery.

grounding: On a rain-shortened cricket ground, children move past a gender stereotype about bowling.

passage:
It was cleaning day in the Pune classroom. The teacher gave out jobs.
"Sweeping is girls' work," said Rudra, pushing the broom at Devika.
Devika pushed it back. "Brooms don't know if you're a boy or a girl."
The class laughed. Rudra shrugged and swept.
Later, when Bhavna was stacking chairs, Rudra tugged her plait as a joke. Bhavna turned. "Don't touch my hair. I don't like it."
Rudra's face went red. "Sorry. I thought it was funny."
"Not to me," said Bhavna.
Rudra nodded and went back to sweeping, faster this time.

qa.q: What was Bhavna doing when Rudra tugged her plait?
qa.a: Stacking chairs.

qa.q: What was Rudra feeling when his face went red?
qa.a: Rudra felt embarrassed and ashamed, realising his joke wasn't funny to Bhavna.

qa.q: What did Devika and Bhavna each do well?
qa.a: Devika challenged the idea that sweeping is girls' work, and Bhavna clearly set a boundary about touching her hair.

qa.q: How might Rudra see his classmates after this?
qa.a: Rudra may see that girls expect the same jobs and respect as boys, and that touching without asking isn't okay.

grounding: In an urban classroom, children challenge a gender stereotype and set a physical boundary.

passage:
"Rudra goes to Kathak class," Ritu whispered to Aadhya. "Dancing in ghungroos like a girl!"
Aadhya frowned. "So?"
"So it's funny."
"Why? My uncle is a Kathak teacher. He's the best in the city."
"Really?"
"Really. And you do karate. Is that funny because it's a boy thing?"
Ritu thought. "No… I'm really good at it."
"Maybe Rudra's really good at Kathak."
Ritu was quiet. At lunch, she asked Rudra, "Can you show us a spin?"
He did. It was very fast. Ritu clapped.

qa.q: Which dance class does Rudra go to?
qa.a: Kathak class.

qa.q: What was Ritu feeling when Aadhya asked about karate?
qa.a: Ritu felt caught out and a bit uncomfortable, noticing her joke didn't make sense.

qa.q: How did Aadhya change Ritu's mind without mocking her?
qa.a: She calmly asked questions and compared it to Ritu's karate, so Ritu saw the stereotype for herself.

qa.q: How might Rudra feel when Ritu asks to see a spin?
qa.a: Rudra probably feels respected and pleased to show his skill, instead of being laughed at.

grounding: Two friends talk through a stereotype about boys doing Kathak.

passage:
I still remember the recess when Charu asked to bowl. We were playing on the back field, and I said, loud enough for everyone, "Careful, she'll bowl like a girl." A few people laughed. I laughed the hardest.
Charu didn't say anything. She just put the ball down and walked to the swings. Her ears were red.
That evening I kept thinking about it. My own cousin plays for the district team, and I would never say that to her. Next day I found Charu by the water tap and said, "That was a mean joke. Sorry." She shrugged, but she was listening.
So at recess I gave her the ball first. She took three wickets, including mine. My name is Aditi, and I don't make that joke anymore.

qa.q: Where was the group playing when Charu asked to bowl?
qa.a: The group was playing on the back field at recess.

qa.q: What does Charu's red ears and walking to the swings suggest she felt?
qa.a: Charu probably felt embarrassed and hurt by the joke, and did not want to show it in front of everyone.

qa.q: What went wrong at first, and what fixed it?
qa.a: Aditi mocked Charu with a stereotype for a laugh; a private, plain apology and giving Charu the ball first began to repair it.

qa.q: If you were one of the kids who laughed, what might change after seeing Charu take three wickets?
qa.a: You might feel a bit foolish and realise the joke was wrong, which could make you less likely to laugh at the next one.

grounding: Illustrates a child recognising that a gender stereotype was mockery and choosing respect and a fair turn instead.

passage:
Teacher's note, Class 4B, school Holi celebration, 13 March
We held a dry-colour Holi on the ground with the rule "ask first". Within minutes a group of boys was chasing some girls with fistfuls of gulal and the girls were shrieking, not all of them happily.
Neelam stepped in front of them and said, "She said no. Ask first, that's the rule." Then she turned to Pema, who was standing aside with clean clothes, and asked, "Do you want colour or not?" Pema said no. One boy called him "delicate", and Neelam said, "He's allowed to say no, same as anyone."
I stopped the game for two minutes and repeated the rule. Afterwards I thanked Neelam in private and spoke to the chasing group about why asking matters for everyone.

qa.q: What was the rule for the dry-colour Holi?
qa.a: The rule was "ask first".

qa.q: How can you tell Neelam felt bothered by the chasing?
qa.a: Neelam stepped in front of the boys and repeated the rule, which suggests she felt uncomfortable and cross that the girls' "no" was being ignored.

qa.q: How could the teacher support the class so Neelam doesn't have to step in alone next time?
qa.a: The teacher could practise asking and accepting "no" with the whole class before any game and keep an adult near the play.

qa.q: What was it like for Pema when Neelam defended his choice?
qa.a: Pema probably felt relieved and respected, because his "no" was treated as normal instead of being mocked as weak.

grounding: Shows a child upholding consent and courtesy for boys and girls alike, and pushing back on mockery, during a festival game.

passage:
Eid holidays, day 2
Dear diary, it's Farida.
Today our class volunteered at the Eid food drive in the community hall. Miss put all the boys on lifting sacks and all the girls on folding packets. I am strong, so I asked to lift. Akash asked to fold, because he likes neat things.
Rizwan laughed and said, "Akash wants to be a girl today." Akash went quiet. I said, "Folding is folding. Lifting is lifting. Nobody's a girl or boy for doing it." Miss heard and said we could swap.
Later Akash asked if he could help me carry the last sack, and he waited until I said yes before he grabbed the other end. That was nice. My arms hurt now but I feel happy. Ammi says I'm her strong girl. 🙂

qa.q: Which job did Farida ask to do at the food drive?
qa.a: Farida asked to lift sacks instead of folding packets.

qa.q: Why did Akash go quiet after Rizwan's joke?
qa.a: Akash likely felt embarrassed and hurt at being mocked for choosing a job he enjoyed.

qa.q: What could Miss do differently at the next volunteer day?
qa.a: Miss could let children choose or rotate jobs instead of splitting them by boys and girls, so nobody has to ask to break a pattern.

qa.q: How might Miss see the swap after hearing Farida?
qa.a: Miss may realise her boys-lift, girls-fold plan was a stereotype and feel glad the children showed her a fairer way.

grounding: Illustrates courtesy across genders: swapping stereotyped jobs, standing up to mockery and asking before helping.

passage:
During the Baisakhi fair in the village, the school held a kabaddi match. Maria, eleven, lined up with the boys' team.
"Girls can't play kabaddi," Amandeep said, and a few boys snickered. "Go do rangoli."
Maria's jaw tightened. "I can. Ask Coach."
Coach nodded. Maria played two raids and got one point. When she was tagged, she stepped back from the line quickly.
Later Amandeep came over. "You were good. Sorry about the rangoli thing." Then he asked, "Can we shake hands, or is that weird?"
"Handshake's fine," Maria said, holding out her hand. His friend Harjit laughed, and Amandeep laughed too.

qa.q: How many points did Maria get in her raids?
qa.a: She got one point.

qa.q: What was Maria feeling when the boys snickered?
qa.a: Maria felt angry and determined, her jaw tight, ready to prove she belonged in the game.

qa.q: What did Amandeep do well after the match?
qa.a: He apologised for the rangoli comment, praised her play, and asked before shaking hands, which respected her boundaries.

qa.q: How might Harjit see the change in Amandeep?
qa.a: Harjit may be amused and a bit surprised to see his friend go from mocking Maria to apologising and treating her as a teammate.

grounding: Shows children learning courtesy and respect across genders instead of stereotyped roles or mockery.
